lesson.title: Reading a Molecule's Electrical Personality
lesson.summary: Molecular polarity describes whether a molecule has a net separation of positive and negative charge, and it depends on both the polarity of individual bonds and the three dimensional shape that arranges them.
lesson.body:
Every covalent bond between two different elements has some degree of charge separation, called a bond dipole, because the more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer to itself. But whether the whole molecule ends up polar is a separate question from whether its bonds are polar. Molecular polarity asks what happens when you add up all of the individual bond dipoles as vectors, quantities with both a size and a direction, and see whether they cancel or leave a net dipole moment. This is why molecular polarity depends directly on molecular geometry: the same set of polar bonds can produce a polar molecule in one shape and a nonpolar molecule in another.

The clearest way to see this is to compare carbon dioxide and water. In CO2, each carbon to oxygen bond is polar, since oxygen is more electronegative than carbon and pulls electron density toward itself. But CO2 is a linear molecule, with the two C=O bond dipoles pointing in exactly opposite directions, 180 degrees apart. Two vectors of equal size pointing opposite ways cancel completely, so CO2 has a net dipole moment of zero even though it is built entirely from polar bonds. Water, by contrast, has two polar O-H bonds, but its geometry is bent, with a bond angle near 104.5 degrees because of the two lone pairs on oxygen. Those two bond dipoles do not point opposite each other, so they only partially cancel, leaving a substantial net dipole moment pointing from the hydrogens toward the oxygen.

This comparison reveals the general rule: symmetry is what allows bond dipoles to cancel. A molecule whose central atom is surrounded by identical atoms in a shape with no lone pairs on the central atom, such as linear CO2, trigonal planar BF3, tetrahedral CH4, or octahedral SF6, will typically be nonpolar because the symmetric arrangement forces the bond vectors to sum to zero. Break that symmetry, either by having different atoms attached, or by having a lone pair replace one of the bonding positions, and the vector sum usually stops canceling, producing a polar molecule.

Determining molecular polarity in practice follows a short procedure. First draw the Lewis structure and use valence shell electron pair repulsion theory to establish the three dimensional geometry. Second, identify which bonds are polar by comparing electronegativities of the bonded atoms; a difference of roughly 0.4 or more usually counts as a meaningfully polar bond. Third, mentally or graphically sum the bond dipole vectors according to the geometry from step one. If the shape is symmetric enough that the vectors cancel, the molecule is nonpolar overall even though it contains polar bonds; if they do not fully cancel, the molecule has a net dipole and is polar.

Molecular polarity is not just a bookkeeping exercise. It is the property that determines whether a substance dissolves in water, how strongly molecules attract their neighbors, and ultimately why some compounds are gases at room temperature while others with similar molar mass are liquids or solids. Every one of the remaining ideas in this chapter, from classifying polar and nonpolar molecules to ranking intermolecular forces, builds directly on the vector reasoning introduced here.
